senses: A cow that produces young.
One who suffers; one who is afflicted.
To rotate inside a monowheel or similar apparatus due to sudden acceleration or braking.
ety: From French gerbille, from Latin gerbo, from Arabic جَرْبُوع (jarbūʕ) or يَرْبُوع (yarbūʕ, “jerboa”). Doublet of jerboa.

senses: A governmental assembly or council in India.
ety: Transliteration of Sanskrit परिषद् (pariṣad) or Hindi परिषद (pariṣad).

senses: Any of a family of Italian hard cheeses made from ewe's milk.
ety: Borrowed from Italian pecorino, from pecora (“sheep”).
examples: Later that evening the two of them sat together in the tiny pantry just off the kitchen, the residue of pecorino cheese and cuts of hanging smoked pork strong and delicious around them.

senses: Shaped like or otherwise resembling a leaf; leaflike.
ety: Learned borrowing from Latin foliātus (“having leaves, leafy, leaved”) (see -ate (adjective-forming suffix)), a participial adjective derived from folium (“leaf; (Late Latin) leaf or sheet of paper”) + -ātus (participial adjective-forming suffix) (ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *bʰleh₃- (“blossom, flower”) or *dʰelh₁- (“to be green”)).

senses: The currency unit of Poland, divided into 100 groszy.
The metaphorical landscape of trends, tastes, etc. promoted by the media.
A large, greatly elongated, type of fish of the family Regalecidae.
examples: For the second time this year an oarfish, a rarely seen deep sea fish that has historically been considered a harbinger of doom, washed up on the California coastline.

senses: Someone who shucks oysters, clams, corn (maize), walnuts, etc.
Someone who shucks or removes something.
A device that shucks produce, such as a corn shucker.
examples: Everyone drank gimlets and the hostess hired an oyster shucker to come up from Baltimore with crates and crates of oysters.

Friends with powerful connections helped him get a corn shucker; he knows of 80 other farmers who are on the waiting list for those machines in a region that is to receive only four during the next two years.

senses: Having three phases.
A genre of German experimental rock music from the 1970s.
examples: Many krautrock bands arose out of the West German student counterculture and connected leftist political activism with experimental rock music and, later, electronic sounds.

senses: That minimises trauma.
That is not resulting from injury or trauma.
ety: From a- + traumatic. First use appears c. 1934.
examples: The need to preserve alveolar bone is paramount and best achieved by atraumatic exodontias including socket compression.

senses: To put (physical) pressure on; to put under pressure.
The events associated with the appointment of a new rector.
examples: This is in direct contrast to Edinburgh, where local shopkeepers and places of entertainment have been known to keep their calendar by university terms and know exactly when graduations, rectorials, and rags take place.

senses: Consisting of, or limited to, letters and/or numbers, especially the characters A to Z (lowercase and uppercase) and 0 to 9.
A bowed string instrument used in the Hindustani classical music of North India.
examples: A sarangi player set the tone and Kalavati began to sing in her sweet, melodious voce; mridangam and sitar accompanied her.

senses: A part of the Earth’s crust that has survived the splitting and merging of continents.
ety: From Ancient Greek κράτος (krátos, “strength, might”). Shortened from original cratogen which was analogical to orogen.

senses: A desire or impulse.
The custom of honoring a family patron saint, celebrated chiefly by the Serbs, but also by some Macedonians, Montenegrins, Bulgarians and Gorani.
ety: From South Slavic slava / слава (slava), literally "fame, glory". The word is also used in some Slavic languages to wish blessings to another person.

senses: The act of evading or going around (bypassing).
The act of prevailing over another by fraud or deception.
ety: From Latin circumventio, equivalent to circumvent + -ion.

senses: Of, coming from, or typical of an author (especially of books)
examples: But no, you have an authorial obligation to determine that this rock is not magical.

senses: A Cuban cocktail made from rum, curaçao, dry vermouth, and grenadine that is stirred or shaken with cracked ice.
A kind of supernatural being, often depicted as having supernatural power, great strength, and frightening appearance; can be a malevolent demon or a beneficent tutelary deity.
The seepage or filtration of a liquid through a porous substance.
The practice of living in one place for a long time.
examples: Where sedentism does occur amongst hunters and gatherers it seems generally to be related to a number of recurrent features.

The implicit correlations between mobility, sedentism, complexity, and progressive evolutionary change are so interwoven and all pervasive as to be all but impossible to disentangle in adaptationist theory.

Assuming sedentism made children less costly, as is often said to be true, our theory predicts a shift toward increased fertility, increased child mortality, decreased food per capita, and increased regional population.

senses: Implied or logically following from something, but not directly stated.
A drug addict who gets a high by inhaling or sniffing (huffing) intoxicating fumes, as in glue or aerosols.
To make volatile; to cause to evaporate.
To make insubstantial; to dissipate.
To become volatile; to evaporate.
A student (or a former student) of a college
ety: From Middle English collegian, from Medieval Latin collēgiānus.

senses: Synonym of ecclesiastical.
ety: From French ecclésial, from Latin ecclēsiālis. By surface analysis, ecclesia + -al.

senses: Toxicity that damages the liver.
Resembling or characteristic of twins.
examples: The Lord parents didn't do cutesy, twinny things with the boys, but Tim admits, “They did some stuff that was a little icky.” Like what? “We had to perform a song together at one of their cocktail parties.”

senses: A topical analgesic and metabolite.
A person who is bored by another; the victim of a bore.
examples: The boree has been heard from frequently since the Renaissance, and his sentiments have undergone little change. The borer hasn't had much to say for himself.

Rennie was an expert on boredom, having done a piece on it for Pandora's “Relationships” column in which she claimed that there were two people involved in boredom, not just one: the borer and the boree.

senses: A cured belly or pork; bacon.
ety: Borrowed from Italian pancetta, from pancia (“belly”).

senses: A salt marsh, or salt pond, enclosed from the sea.
An ancient ivory hunting-horn.
ety: From Middle English olifaunt, from Anglo-Norman oliphant (“ivory, elephant”) and Old French oliphant (“ivory, elephant, musical horn of ivory”), from Latin elephantus (“elephant”), from Ancient Greek ἐλέφας (eléphas, “ivory, elephant”).

senses: The act of facilitating or making easy.
Confused, perplexed or flustered.
examples: He's good at what he knows, but he gets completely flummoxed when new problems arise.
